title: The table and the tablecloth today
word: The table and the tablecloth today
hookLine: Karo's code with Isserles' notes, still the reference rabbis reach for
last: A WHOLE LIFE FITS IN FOUR ROWS.

lines: A SECOND VOICE ON THE PAGE.
I HAVE SET THE LORD ALWAYS BEFORE ME.
cards: A code of law that begins in bed. Its first ruling is about waking up: a person should rise like a lion in the morning to serve the Creator, and be the one who wakes the dawn. Not the dawn waking you.
You waking it. That's the opening of a book by Rabbi Joseph Karo.
And on the same page, set off from his words, a second rabbi adds a line before Karo's lion even gets out of bed, a verse from the Psalms: "I have set the LORD always before me."
Two voices, one page, and the page is still open on desks today.

teach.h: THE SET TABLE: LAW, READY TO USE.
teach.b: You met this pair last year; today, the page as it's used now. First, the table. Karo called his code the Shulchan Arukh, the set table: the law laid out and ready, like a meal with every dish in its place.
He had already written a long commentary weighing the earlier authorities, and this was its short, usable form, in brief rulings, following yesterday's four rows. Second, the tablecloth.
In Poland, Rabbi Moses Isserles, known as the Rema, saw that in places the set table didn't match the practice of his own Ashkenazi communities, since Karo had leaned on Sephardi authorities.
So he didn't write a rival book. He wrote notes, and called them the Mappah, the tablecloth, spread over Karo's table.
Third, the page. The two are printed together, Karo's ruling and then, set off, the Rema's gloss.
Where they differ, Sephardi communities generally look to Karo and Ashkenazi communities to the Rema: two traditions sharing one table. Fourth, today.
The Shulchan Arukh is printed surrounded by commentaries, and a rabbi answering an everyday question about Shabbat, a kosher kitchen or a business dispute may well start there.
Over time the table has collected many guests, all arguing politely around the edges. But open it, and it still begins the same way: rise like a lion, and above it, the Rema's line.

how: Rabbis and students consult the Shulchan Arukh, printed with the Rema's glosses and later commentaries, when answering questions of daily practice; it is also a core text for those studying toward rabbinic ordination.

games.q: you're Moses Isserles. a strong new code arrives, but in places its rulings don't match your community's practice. what do you do?
o: write a rival code from scratch.
add notes on the same page, recording your community's practice.
games.why: he writes glosses, the tablecloth, spread over Karo's set table. the two traditions are printed together.

practice: Choose a question from your own ordinary day: how to begin the morning, what to say before eating, how soon to pay someone who works for you.
Just hold it, and notice how ordinary it is, and that a whole tradition thought it worth an answer.
